name: Pedro Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm the business reporter for a regional news outlet, so my patch is the port, the two big food factories, the retail park and a lot of small firms nobody else writes about. I start around eight with an AI tool that skims the overnight company filings, planning applications and court insolvency lists, and flags anything with a local name in it. Then it's calls, a site visit if I can get one, and two or three stories filed by six. On Thursdays I also put together our business newsletter, which goes to about nine thousand inboxes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the first person to spot that a firm on the industrial estate is quietly in trouble, before the staff know. I like the port people, honestly, the crane drivers and the shipping agents, because they'll tell you how the economy is really doing. What wears me out is the clicks target, because a story about a bakery chain closing gets ten times the readers of a careful one about wages. I live with Ana, my partner, who's a physiotherapist, and we've got about four months of money put aside, so I'm not desperate, but I'm not relaxed either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Mostly hype. I can picture that, because half the pitches I get from tech firms already sound like hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the tools are useful for grunt work and that's about it. I'd probably write a column about all the local firms that paid consultants for an AI plan and got a chatbot nobody uses. Online I'd keep it light and a bit smug, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a little disappointed, because I've built my working habits around these tools getting better. But my job would be fine. The business desk actually makes money for the outlet, because the newsletter carries sponsors, so I'm one of the safer people in the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and push the newsletter harder, maybe a second edition on Mondays with a jobs and openings roundup. I'd ask for a raise once the sponsor numbers come in, around March when budgets are set. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe two hundred, so we can think about buying a flat in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. The pressures in local news don't go away, but they're the pressures I already know how to live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the clicks target. Does that get easier or harder in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About the same. The target goes up a bit every year whatever happens with AI, and Martina (my editor) passes it on with an apologetic face. I've learned to pair a quick popular story with the slow one I actually care about, so the numbers carry the good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If someone at the outlet were going to struggle even in this quiet version, who would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the sub-editors, the people who check and tidy copy, because even a little automation chips at their hours. There's a guy called Rob who's been subbing for twenty years and already does half his shifts on the sports pages. The routine bits AI does take in this picture are exactly his bits.

say: The tools are fine for **grunt work**, and that's all they turned out to be.
Local firms paid for **AI plans** and mostly got chatbots nobody uses.
think: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because my habits assume the tools keep getting better.
The **business desk** makes money, so I'm one of the safer people in the building.
do: Launch a **Monday edition** of the business newsletter with a jobs and openings roundup.
Ask for a **raise** in March, once the sponsor figures for the newsletter are in.
Keep saving about **two hundred** a month towards a flat with Ana.
feel: **Relaxed**, because the pressures in local news are ones he already knows how to handle.
S0.quote: The business desk actually makes money for the outlet, because the newsletter carries sponsors, so I'm one of the safer people in the building.
fieldNote: He sees himself as **protected** because his desk brings in sponsor money.
His worry turns quickly to **colleagues**, especially Rob, a long-serving sub-editor.
He's slightly **disappointed** the tools stall, which shows how much he relies on them.
The **clicks target** is a background pressure he treats as normal, not new.

steps.text: Launch a Monday edition of the business newsletter with a jobs roundup
Ask for a raise in March using the newsletter sponsor figures
Put about two hundred a month towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. This one I believe more. This is basically the next three years if you ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the business desk should be first to use it properly, not last. I'd pitch myself as the person who sets up the tools for the whole newsroom, because I already use them every day. Online I'd say local news can survive this if it uses the time saved to get out of the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the outlet will hire fewer reporters and lean on people like me who can turn out more with the tools. That's good for me and bad for the people who can't or won't. My job probably gets bigger and my pay probably doesn't, which is the classic deal in this business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd write a short guide for the newsroom on which tools to trust for filings, transcripts and data, and run a lunchtime session. I'd build a paid alert service for local businesses, say fifteen a month, that flags planning and insolvency news for their area. Within the year I'd ask to be called business and data editor, and ask for the pay to match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a buzz, if I'm honest. There's a little guilt under it, because my good year might be someone else's bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your good year might be someone else's bad one. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob (the sub-editor) again, and also Jess, who writes the council round-up from meeting minutes. Software could draft Jess's round-up in a minute, and the outlet will notice. I'd want to bring Jess onto the data side with me, but I don't control the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part of your own job you'd hand to the software first, and what would you never hand over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand over the first draft of results stories, like 'the factory's profits fell eight percent', without a second thought. I would never hand over the phone call to the shift worker at the factory gate who tells me the night shift is being cut. Software can read a filing, but a filing doesn't tell you about the night shift.

say: The business desk should be **first** to use these tools properly, not last.
Local news survives if the **time saved** goes into getting out of the office.
think: The outlet will hire **fewer reporters** and lean on people who can produce more.
His job likely gets **bigger**, while his pay probably stays the same.
do: Write a **newsroom guide** to trusted tools and run a lunchtime training session.
Build a **paid alert service** for local firms at about fifteen a month.
Ask within the year to become **business and data** editor, with matching pay.
feel: A **buzz** of opportunity, with a little **guilt** about colleagues.
S1.quote: Software can read a filing, but a filing doesn't tell you about the night shift.
fieldNote: He casts himself as the newsroom's **tools person** and sees a career step in it.
His worry is for **Rob and Jess**, whose routine writing is easiest to automate.
He's clear about which work to keep: the **human sources** at the factory gate.
He accepts the old trade of **more work**, same pay, without much anger.

steps.text: Write a newsroom guide to AI tools and run a lunchtime session
Start a fifteen-a-month planning and insolvency alert service for local firms
Ask to become business and data editor with a pay rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's my newsletter, my results stories and my filings scanning, all of it, inside two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say people still want to know which human is telling them the port is laying off two hundred people. I'd say it calmly, because panicking in public doesn't help anyone. I'd probably also say governments should have seen this coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job as it is now is gone by about 2029. Almost everything I do is thinking work, reading, writing and checking, and that's the first thing that goes in this picture. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, because there's almost nothing hands-on in my day except driving to the port.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by turning my sources into something I own: a small paid local business briefing under my own name, with events where firm owners meet in person. I'd move savings into a separate account and cut the eating out, so we'd have six months rather than four by the time it lands. In the first year after, I'd try to sell myself as the person who checks and stands behind what the machines write, because someone still has to sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest, but it's a busy kind of scared. I'd rather be running than standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned events where firm owners meet in person. Why does the in-person part matter to you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's the one thing in my job that's physical. A room above the rugby club with forty business owners and bad coffee is something a machine can't host for another few years at least. Maybe people won't want a machine to host it, either. If the writing goes in 2028, the room is what I'd still have in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana the night you decided this was really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her my salary might be gone in a year, and that her physio work is the steadier one now, which flips how we've always talked about it. Then I'd tell her I have a plan and show her the spreadsheet. Ana (my partner) would ask what the plan is if the plan fails, and I wouldn't have a great answer.

say: People still want a **named human** telling them the port is laying people off.
Governments should have **seen this coming** and prepared.
think: His job as it is now is likely **gone by 2029**.
Almost all his day is **thinking work**, so the robot delay doesn't help him.
do: Start a **paid business briefing** under his own name, with in-person owner events.
Cut eating out and build savings from four to **six months**.
Sell himself as the person who **checks and signs** machine-written business news.
feel: **Scared**, but it's a busy fear that pushes him to act.
S2.quote: A room above the rugby club with forty business owners and bad coffee is something a machine can't host for another few years at least.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his current job** around 2029 and says so plainly.
He grabs the one **physical** part of his work, hosting people in a room.
He notices that Ana's **physio job** becomes the household's safer income.
He has a plan but no **fallback** if the plan fails, and admits it.

steps.text: Launch a paid local business briefing with in-person owner events
Move savings to a separate account until there's six months' cover
Cut eating out and takeaways to two a month
Pitch himself to firms as an editor who checks AI-written news

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels like enough to build something, but not enough to dither.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as the two-year version, but I'd sound more confident, because five years is time to show it can work. I'd probably write about it, a series on how the port and the factories are planning for it. That's good journalism and good positioning for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I've got maybe three good years left of the current job, then two of it shrinking. That's enough time to make my own name worth paying for. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, which isn't old, but I'd want my next thing running well before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the paid business briefing next spring and aim for three hundred paying readers by the end of year two. I'd do a short course in business finance, probably evenings, so I can read company accounts properly instead of leaning on the tool. Ana and I would hold off on buying a flat and keep renting, so our savings stay in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a manageable way. Five years is the version where I feel like I can still steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on buying a flat. How does that land at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not brilliantly. Ana has wanted to buy since we moved in, and her mum keeps sending us listings. But a mortgage on a reporter's salary that might vanish in five years is a bet I don't want to make yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Of the people you've met through work, who do you think gets through this best?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shipping agents at the port, I think. Half of their job is phoning people and knowing who owes who a favour, and that's hard to automate. I'd probably end up learning more from them than from any course.

say: Five years is **time to show** a local business briefing can work.
He'd write a **series** on how the port and factories are planning ahead.
think: He has about **three good years** in the current job, then two of decline.
He wants his **next thing** running well before he's thirty-two.
do: Launch the **paid briefing** next spring, aiming for 300 readers in two years.
Take an evening course in **business finance** to read accounts himself.
Keep **renting** and hold savings in cash instead of buying a flat.
feel: **Nervous** but manageable, because five years still feels steerable.
S3.quote: A mortgage on a reporter's salary that might vanish in five years is a bet I don't want to make yet.
fieldNote: He treats the five years as a **runway** to build his own paid product.
The **flat** is where his plan rubs against Ana's hopes and her mother's listings.
He admires the **port agents** for relationships that are hard to automate.
His mood is anxious, not alarmed, because he feels he has **time to act**.

steps.text: Launch the paid briefing next spring and aim for 300 readers
Take an evening business finance course to read company accounts
Delay buying a flat with Ana and keep renting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Same ending, but I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career chapter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and that people in my trade who complain have had a decade's warning. I'd say it less harshly at work, because some colleagues would take it personally. I'd probably keep writing about the local economy getting ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means my career in reporting has an end date, and I can plan around it. Ten years is enough to get properly good at something next door to journalism, like advising firms on how to talk to the public, or running events. I'd still worry, because a decade passes fast and I tend to say yes to too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and build the briefing slowly, as a side thing that pays for holidays at first. I'd probably buy the flat with Ana after all, maybe in two years, because there's time to pay a chunk off. Around year six or seven I'd decide whether the briefing or a communications job is my next main income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two. There's a low hum of worry, but it's the kind I can live alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you tend to say yes to too much. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like me agreeing to run the newsroom tools, the newsletter, the briefing and a podcast, and then doing all of them badly. Martina (my editor) has already told me once to pick two things. With ten years, the danger is I spread myself thin instead of picking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra decade change anything for Ana and you beyond the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably kids, if I'm honest. With two years I wouldn't want to bring a baby into a house where my income is about to vanish. With ten, I'd feel okay saying yes to that conversation in a few years.

say: Ten years is **plenty of warning** for anyone in his trade.
He'd keep writing about the **local economy** getting ready.
think: His reporting career now has an **end date** he can plan around.
He could move into **communications** or events, next door to journalism.
do: Keep the job and grow the **briefing slowly** as a side income.
Buy a **flat** with Ana in about two years.
Choose by year seven between the briefing and a **communications job**.
feel: Calmer, with a **low hum** of worry he can live with.
S4.quote: With two years I wouldn't want to bring a baby into a house where my income is about to vanish.
fieldNote: The decade lets him **reopen plans** for a flat and possibly children.
He knows his own weakness: **spreading thin** across too many projects.
His job still has an end date, so he stays anxious, but with **real control**.
He's harsher about colleagues in private, calling it a **decade's warning**.

steps.text: Keep the reporting job and grow the briefing slowly
Run the briefing as paid side work that covers holidays
Buy a flat with Ana in about two years
Decide by year seven on a move into communications work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Everything I do for money is thinking work, and two years isn't enough time to build something of my own that pays the rent. What would help is some kind of bridge income while people retrain, and honestly, local firms and councils still paying for named, local news instead of switching it all to free machine copy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the local news once the machines can write it. If a big tech firm or a national chain owns the only local feed, nobody checks the council or the port. I'd rather pay for a local reporter I can phone than read a free one I can't.

headlineQuote: I'd rather pay for a local reporter I can phone than read a free one I can't.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** business reporter covering a port, factories and small firms for a regional outlet.
He uses AI **every day** to scan filings and planning lists, and sees himself as the newsroom's tools person.
He rents with Ana, a **physiotherapist**, and has about four months of savings.
His instinct in every scenario is to build a **paid business briefing** under his own name.
Short timelines push him to **save and cut back**; the ten-year version reopens a flat and children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his work is almost all thinking work and two years is too short.
whatWouldHelp: Local firms and councils still paying for **named local news**.
